chain.g: image, artistic representation of a thing

ety.text: From Latin īcōn, from Ancient Greek εἰκών (eikṓn, “likeness, image, portrait”). Eastern Orthodox Church sense is attested from 1833. Computing sense first recorded in 1982.

senses.d: An image, symbol, picture, portrait, or other representation, usually as an object of religious devotion.
A type of religious painting portraying a saint or scene from Scripture, often done on wooden panels.
ex: Last week the Archdiocese sent emmissaries to investigate the icon and decided that the tears were not a hoax, Father Koufos said.

senses.d: A person or thing that is the best example of a certain profession or some doing.
ex: That man is an icon in the business; he personifies loyalty and good business sense.

senses.d: A small picture that represents something.
ex: Click the loudspeaker icon to configure audio settings.

senses.d: An image used to represent a user; an avatar or profile picture.
ex: Is it okay if I use your drawing as my icon?

senses.d: A word, character, or sign whose form reflects and is determined by the referent; onomatopoeic words are necessarily all icons.

ety.text: Borrowed from Russian икона (ikona, “(Eastern Orthodox) religious image”) [1859]; in the GUI sense from English icon, ultimately from Ancient Greek εἰκών (eikṓn, “figure, image, etc.”).
From Ancient Greek εἰκών (eikṓn, “likeness, image, portrait”). Doublet of ancona.

ety.text: Borrowed from French icône, from Russian ико́на (ikóna), from Ancient Greek εἰκών (eikṓn), εἰκόνος (eikónos, “image, likeness”).

ety.text: From Old Galician-Portuguese idolo, borrowed from Latin īdōlum, from Ancient Greek εἴδωλον (eídōlon, “image, idol”), from εἶδος (eîdos, “form”), from Proto-Indo-European *weyd- (“to see”).
From Late Latin īconicus, from Ancient Greek εἰκονικός (eikonikós). By surface analysis, icon + -ic.

senses.d: Relating to, or having the characteristics of, an icon.

ex: an iconic move in martial arts

senses.d: Famously and distinctively representative of its type.
ex: For younger musicians, Coltrane’s death became one of those iconic events that stays vividly in the mind.
She angrily turned, giving me my favorite view, that iconic view of a woman from the rear.
an iconic gesture in sign language

ety.text: Borrowed from Latin iconicus, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek εἰκονικός (eikonikós). Morphologically, from icône + -ique.
